contract: make_forecaster(training_returns, names) -> object with forecast() and update(returns). training_returns is a (7280, 50) float array of daily returns (decimal) from 1971-03-12 to 1999-12-31: column 0 is the CRSP value-weighted market (Mkt-RF + RF), columns 1-49 the value-weighted Fama-French industries; names lists the 50 series. The evaluator then walks through the 6,475 trading days 2000-01-03..2025-09-30: forecast() must return a (50,) array of next-day return variances in [1e-10, 1]; afterwards update(r) receives that day's (50,) returns. Score: mean QLIKE loss log(h) + r^2/h over all days and series (minimize); the RiskMetrics EWMA benchmark (lambda 0.94), the difference and a Diebold-Mariano statistic are reported. The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process: numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas and the other installed packages are importable, while the evaluator's library, its data files, the network and subprocesses are not accessible; one thread and 3 GB of memory. It receives only the arguments described here, one call at a time: the arguments of a call are sent after the value of the previous call has been received. Arguments and return values travel as numbers, strings, lists, dicts with string keys and numeric numpy arrays, so a tuple arrives as a list
notes: Out-of-sample comparison of daily variance forecasts in the spirit of Hansen and Lunde (2005), with squared daily returns as the volatility proxy and the QLIKE loss, which Patton (2011) shows ranks forecasts consistently with such noisy proxies. The evaluator enforces causality by revealing each day's returns only after that day's forecasts. Local references: rolling 63-day variance (seed) -7.563, RiskMetrics -7.6125, GARCH(1,1) and GJR-GARCH(1,1) estimated on 1990-1999 and kept fixed -7.598 and -7.610. No published number is reproduced: Hansen and Lunde use other assets, intraday realized-variance proxies and other periods.

name: Finance: Daily volatility forecasting for US equity portfolios
description: Forecast the next day's return variance of the US stock market and 49 industry portfolios, updating the forecasts day by day from 2000 to 2025 after a training period ending in 1999. The evaluator reveals each day's returns only after the forecasts are made and scores the QLIKE loss against squared returns.
benchmark: Finance: Daily volatility forecasting for US equity portfolios
paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

sources.locator: Hansen and Lunde (2005): out-of-sample comparison of many volatility models against GARCH(1,1) with several loss functions.
Patton (2011): loss functions, including QLIKE, that rank volatility forecasts consistently when the true variance is replaced by a noisy proxy such as the squared return.
Bollerslev (1986): the GARCH model, the classic benchmark for conditional variance forecasts.
Daily Fama/French factors (market = Mkt-RF + RF) and value-weighted 49 industry portfolio returns, CRSP 202509 files pinned in catalog/finance-data-lock.json.

limitations: Squared daily returns are a noisy proxy for the daily variance; QLIKE ranks forecasts consistently with this proxy but the loss level is not a variance-accuracy measure, and intraday realized variances are not available here.
Forecasts are for close-to-close total returns (no mean adjustment); weekends, holidays and overnight effects are treated like any other trading day.

The evaluation period 2000-2025 is public. A candidate that reads the prepared files or memorizes returns can look ahead; the interface only passes returns up to the previous day. Treat scores as development scores.
One data vintage of CRSP value-weighted portfolio returns is used; the 50 series are strongly correlated, so they do not provide 50 independent comparisons.

The candidate runs in a sandboxed child process that never receives later data, realised outcomes or reference solutions; module-level code still runs once in the evaluator process when the shared template imports the candidate, and outside macOS (kernel sandbox) deliberately hostile native code could bypass the file policy.
